passage:
Tuesday. "Every game needs a finish line," said Salma, chewing her pencil. Nirmala frowned. "We keep arguing about how to move." "Because we don't know what we're moving for," said Salma. "First: how does someone win?"

Thursday. In the playground the group agreed: each team hides flags in its half, and whichever team gathers five flags first wins.

Saturday. Now the rules came easily. Runners could step only on the chalk squares, and nobody could carry more than one flag. "If we knew the goal on Tuesday," Nirmala laughed, "we'd have saved two days."

qa.q: How many flags does a team need to win?
qa.a: A team needs five flags to win.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling about the arguments on Tuesday?
qa.a: Nirmala was frustrated, since the group kept arguing about moves without a shared goal.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the group have used on Tuesday, and why?
qa.a: They could have borrowed rules from a known game and tested them with a short trial, since that gives a starting point. Starting with the goal still helped make later choices simple.

qa.q: How do the runners' rules look to someone who joins late?
qa.a: A newcomer would see clear limits, such as the chalk squares and one flag at a time, and could join without asking the whole story because the goal is simple.

grounding: A girl points out a game needs an end, the group sets the first-to-five-flags goal and builds movement rules around it.

passage: Kamal, your new game has no end, so everyone just runs till they fight. Let your Kalyani Paati tell you something. When I was ten, in our street in Thanjavur, we made up games every evening, and they always fell apart. One day I said, 'Wait. How does anyone win?' Nobody knew. So we decided that first: five flags, made from old saree bits, hidden at each end. First team to bring home all five wins. Only then did we make the other rules: you carry one flag at a time, and you can be caught only on the other side. That game lasted all summer, and we even taught it to my cousins from Madurai.

qa.q: What were the flags made from?
How might young Kalyani have felt when the games kept falling apart?
qa.a: She was likely frustrated and puzzled, which led her to ask how anyone wins.

qa.q: What was the key choice in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Deciding the goal first, five flags, so every other rule could be built to serve that end.

qa.q: How did the other children in the street experience the new game?
qa.a: They got a game with a clear finish that lasted all summer, good enough to teach to the cousins from Madurai.

grounding: Shows a girl insisting a game needs an end, her group settling on five flags to win, and then building the movement rules around it.

passage: Recess was only twenty minutes, and half the ground was taken by the older kids' cricket, so Sarita's group had a strip of grass by the wall. Tushar was already explaining rules: "You run here, then you jump there, then..." "Stop," Sarita said. "How does someone win? Games have to finish somehow, or we'll just run around till the bell." Everyone looked at her. "Five flags," she said. "Our handkerchiefs, five each side. First team to steal all five wins." Then the rest came quickly: you can take only one at a time; if you're tagged on their side, you freeze. When the bell rang, Tushar's team had four, and they were already planning a rematch.

qa.q: Why did Sarita say 'Stop' to Tushar?
qa.a: She was impatient with rules that had no end and worried they'd just run around till the bell.

qa.q: What does Sarita's approach suggest for making any game?
qa.a: Decide how someone wins first, then build the other rules around that goal, so the game makes sense quickly.

qa.q: How might Tushar see Sarita cutting in?
qa.a: Tushar was mid-explanation, but his team got four flags and wanted a rematch, so he seems to have enjoyed the game she shaped.

grounding: Illustrates a girl saying a game needs an end, the group choosing five flags as the goal, and building the other rules around it.
